title: Respecting Other People's Time
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article treats time management as a relationship issue rather than a scheduling one, arguing that how leaders handle other people's time reveals and shapes how much respect they command. It lays out concrete behaviors, from starting meetings on time to not volunteering colleagues without asking, that either build or erode trust. The piece points out that colleagues often mock leaders privately for chronic time disrespect, even when it stems from disorganization rather than malice. It closes by framing respect for others' time as a mirror of self-respect and a quiet but powerful form of leadership modeling.
points: How a leader treats other people's time is a strong, visible signal of respect or disrespect.
Colleagues who feel their time is disrespected often mock the leader behind their back.
Concrete habits like starting and ending meetings on time and giving notice when running late matter a great deal.
Volunteering other people's time without asking them is called out as especially disrespectful.
Respecting others' time schedules ultimately models respect for one's own time as well.
quotes: Chief among the issues that display respect or disrespect is how leaders treat other people's time.
We don't fully trust leaders who disrespect us, even when this contempt is unintentional or as a result of disorganization.
Perhaps most damning is the fact that colleagues treat those who consistently disrespect their time with contempt, often mocking them when they aren't present.
Delaying a meeting because of a leader's lateness is not only rude, but instantly devalues the time of others.
Maybe the most disrespectful time-related action a leader can engage in is volunteering other people's time without asking them.
Leaders who give the respect regarding time that they want to receive usually end up becoming powerful role models for others.
